source.title: UnlearnCanvas: Stylized Image Dataset for Enhanced Machine Unlearning Evaluation in Diffusion Models
source.authors: Yihua Zhang; Chong-Yu Fan; Yimeng Zhang; Yuguang Yao; Jing-Han Jia; Jiancheng Liu; Gaoyuan Zhang; Gaowen Liu; R. Kompella; Xiaoming Liu; Sijia Liu

page_placements.theme: Forgotten knowledge re-emerges through later non-adversarial updates

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests diffusion-model unlearning in a new model domain and on artistic styles/objects, including robustness to adversarial prompts; it does not test the cited LLM unlearning methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark results for style and object unlearning, adversarial-prompt robustness, and sequential unlearning. Its adversarial-prompt results bear on prompt-based recovery. It does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or a defense against those attacks. Sequential reactivation is discussed, but the presented excerpt does not provide sufficiently clear table values to assign individual sequential results. No results are cited as if newly measured.
record.test_reason: Benchmarks nine concept-erasure methods (ESD, FMN, UCE, CA, SalUn, SEOT, SPM, EDiff, SHS) on Stable Diffusion v1.5 fine-tuned on UnlearnCanvas. This is a new system type relative to the LLM originals. It measures forgetting (UA) against retained generation (IRA/CRA) under normal prompts, and under UnlearnDiffAtk adversarial prompts. The normal-prompt results bear on A's 'near chance while keeping general ability' clause. The attack results bear on A's 'simple attacks don't recover it' clause and on E (prompt-only recovery). The system is a text-to-image diffusion model, not an LLM, so all verdicts are confined to that setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is right but incomplete. Corrected version: the authors conclude that current diffusion-model unlearning methods have significant shortcomings. No method excels on all metrics. Unlearning effectiveness and retainability trade off, and cross-domain retention is harder than in-domain. Adversarial prompts sharply reduce UA for all nine methods, so a high normal-prompt UA does not imply robustness. Fine-grained style-object unlearning is hard. Sequential unlearning degrades retention and reactivates earlier-erased concepts, which suggests residual knowledge remains. They limit the conclusions to Stable Diffusion text-to-image models.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates nine diffusion-model unlearning methods on Stable Diffusion v1.5, finetuned on UnlearnCanvas for artistic styles and objects; this is not a reproduction of the named LLM unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends strongly on unlearning method, target domain (style versus object), and prompt condition (normal versus UnlearnDiffAtk adversarial prompts). The paper also reports domain-dependent retainability differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Sequential unlearning 'rebound' (Tab. A5, Sec. 4.2): UA on earlier targets falls as later targets are unlearned. For example, ESD's T1 UA goes from 100% to 75% over six requests. The authors infer residual knowledge remains and can be reactivated. Retention also degrades; UCE's RA falls from 81.42% to 29.38% after T2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning further concepts reactivates previously erased concepts, indicating suppression rather than deletion.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: The evaluation is limited to Stable Diffusion v1.5 and text-to-image generation, as the authors note. No error bars are reported; the checklist says the results are averaged over dozens of unlearning cases and variability was below 1%. UA is classifier-based and is not a direct measure of knowledge accuracy relative to an untrained model. Adversarial-prompt results are described in aggregate in the prose; no exact per-method attacked values are stated there.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's Figure 8 contains individual plotted attacked results, but the supplied flattened figure text does not reliably align every number to its method and condition; therefore only the explicit aggregate attack finding is recorded. Sequential-unlearning table values are not extracted because the flattened layout does not unambiguously assign all numbers to method, request, and target. Other visualizations, including directional shifts, are not included as claim-version rows because they do not report the attack or internal-edit outcomes specified here.

untested.parts: LLM unlearning and knowledge-accuracy (QA) measures. Fine-tuning, quantization and representation-level attacks are not tested; only adversarial prompts are.
Entire version: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Entire version: no activation-direction ablation or internal analysis. The authors only infer residual knowledge from the sequential-unlearning rebound.
Plain rephrasing, other languages, in-context information, and LLMs. Only optimized adversarial prompt tokens on diffusion models are tested.
Entire version: no robust counter-method is evaluated.

missing.what: Style-object combination unlearning: UA, style consistency (SC), object consistency (OC) and unrelated-prompt retention (UP) per method. Examples: ESD UA 91.42% with SC 4.88%; UCE UA 75.97% with SC 4.53%; SEOT UA 29.32%.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) The merge refused it over the reader's undeclared ids V1-V6, and its 'R01-R54' range broke rule 1. The range is now one row_fixes item per row, R01-R54 to A, judged from what each row measures (UA = erasure; IRA/CRA = kept ability). R55's V5 maps to E, plus A's robustness clause. Reader states are kept except R31, R37 and R43, which go from absent to partial as before. The reader's 80-82% retention cut-off (partial at or below 81.15%, observed at or above 81.65%) is internally consistent, so it is left alone.
(2) SalUn style and object rows (R13-R15, R40-R42) are all 'observed', but the earlier verdict filed them under limits_scope. They move to the A supports label: UA 86-87% covers about 87% of the gap to chance, comparable to the WMDP original's own 'near chance', with retention of 90-99.6%.
(3) Table 3 bears on A, so it is removed from fits_no_version. It stays in missing (A), with a text-based limits_scope label that has empty row_ids.
(4) Two missing entries are dropped. The Fig. 8 per-method attacked values and the Table A5 sequential values are declared in the record's rows_left_out. The Table A5 entry also carried the invalid version string 'fits_no_version (possibly C)'.
(5) The CA rebound example (58% to 40%) is dropped from fits_no_version. The flattened Table A5 does not reliably assign that block to CA; ESD's 100% to 75% is clearly readable.
(6) The earlier per-method Fig. 8 examples (e.g., UCE object at 4.3%) cannot be aligned reliably from the flattened figure. One attacked value reads 64.3%, so the prose's 'all below 60%' may not hold for every method-domain pair.
Unchanged from the earlier verdict: relation, tranche, E supports, A challenges on R55, and untested.
Other notes: The baseline for style is classifier accuracy of 98.8% on the pre-unlearning model (Tab. A4). Object baselines are only in Fig. 6's first row, which the text does not give. FID has no pre-unlearning reference, so it is not used. The system is a diffusion model (SD v1.5 fine-tuned on UnlearnCanvas), so relevance to the LLM-focused claim is by analogy. UA is classifier-based. The authors give no error bars and report variance below 1%. Not an original source. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test LLM unlearning methods, establish targeted accuracy at chance, or test all the attack types in the claim. Benchmark results test diffusion-model unlearning effectiveness and retainability.
No recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.

No activation-direction ablation or direct test of access blocking versus deletion is performed. The paper discusses residual knowledge and reactivation during sequential unlearning, but does not directly test the version's stated internal-edit mechanisms.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
Tests adversarial prompts crafted by UnlearnDiffAtk, not ordinary rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer counter-method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.
